doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Career reflections and retiring the lying-down routine
summary: Havens reflects on a rewarding career of playing with his idols, continuing to freelance, and the origin of his trademark routine.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: No, I’ve had a very rewarding career. All the people that I used to hear on records, the individual jazz players, I’ve been able to play with most of them in my own time, and it’s just been a wonderful experience. And I’m still, up to this year, I’ve been freelancing in the jazz concerts and jazz parties, and it’s still continuing to be a lot of fun as well as financially rewarding too.
Well I hope it continues for you.

Well I hope so too. Well I had sort of semi-retired myself a few years ago. But I’m discovering that I’m not quite as happy just sitting around the house listening to records as I have been doing actual performing. So I think I may just keep up as long as I can physically hold the horn I’ll probably play.
Good. But maybe you shouldn’t do the thing on your back.

No, I tried to retire that completely, until they called me to the theatre there. And now I’ve already, this year, laid on my back 150 times, and I have that many more to go. But I’m going to draw the line after this year.
It was such a serendipitous thing that you did that one night.

Just as a joke one night, and it’s continued throughout my career. And now when somebody comes up to me and says, “You’re one of my favorite trombone player and do you still do that number where you lay on the floor” that’s always the first thing they can think of.
